title: Mark Sumner of the University of Leeds explains the challenges facing the fashion industry

paragraphs.text: The fashion industry has some major sustainability problems. It is predicted that within the next 10 to 15 years the industry's water consumption will reach 118 billion cubic metres, its carbon footprint will increase to 2,791 million tonnes and the amount of waste it creates will soar to 148 million tonnes. These predictions for the industry as a whole are in spite of significant progress being made by brands and retailers to reduce their impact. Many are using sustainable cotton initiatives to reduce water, energy and chemical use, new dyeing technology to reduce water use by up to 50%, as well as numerous energy and chemical saving schemes throughout the supply chain. In the UK, the result of these initiatives is filtering through to stores to a limited extent, with a reduction in the carbon and water footprints per tonne of clothing of 8% and 7% respectively being achieved over the last five years.

By these means, the industry has succeeded in reducing the environmental footprint of its products. But the problem has now shifted to the consumption side: the insatiable appetite for fashion means people are buying more and more clothes. Over the last five years, there has been a 10% increase in the amount of clothing purchased in the UK alone. And not only are consumers buying more; more of their clothing gets discarded more quickly as they chase the latest fashion trends. It is estimated there is over £30 billion of clothing sitting in wardrobes across the UK that hasn't been used for over 12 months.

Catering for this appetite for the latest trends, or 'fast fashion' as it is sometimes called, is seen by many as the fundamental cause of all the sustainability issues that the industry faces. It has been suggested by numerous commentators that ethical consumerism can and will lead to a radical shift in behaviour. Over time, it is thought, 'slow fashion' will become the norm, with consumers wearing garments of a timeless and classical style that last for ten years. This, so commentators say, will minimise the need to make new purchases of the latest fashion fad, thereby reducing impacts. Unfortunately, this argument is predicated on the mistaken assumption that consumers make rational choices.

The undeniable fact is that the predicted growth of ethical consumerism has not materialised in mainstream fashion. Ethically minded brands believe the single biggest issue stopping them becoming more sustainable is the consumer, either through people's lack of awareness of the issues faced by the industry, or through a reluctance to pay the premium for sustainable products.

It is also important to realise that marketing tools such as questionnaires and surveys used to predict the growth of ethical consumption are problematic. They are good for identifying purchase intention, but poor for predicting actual behaviour. Surveys tend to elicit a response that presents the participant in a positive light: non-ethical shoppers tend to state they are ethical to protect their external image. And surveys depend on the participant being truthful and knowledgeable about their behaviour.
How truthful we are is debatable, and research shows we are not as knowledgeable as we think we are about the drivers of our behaviour.

Not only is our behaviour more selfish than we might like to believe, it is also less rational. An ethical consumer will make considered judgements about purchases on the best outcome in terms of costs and benefits for themselves and the environment. But consumption, and in particular fashion consumption, is quite irrational. Purchase decisions are more likely to be driven by desires linked to pleasure and excitement. Fashion is a social activity for establishing our status, but it is also an activity that is driven by emotional desires such as the fantasy, excitement and aspiration of living a better, more fulfilling life.

Ethical campaigners, journalists and even some brands have argued that consumers would be able to overcome these subconscious forces if they had more information. But evidence shows that this does little to increase ethical behaviour. In fact, the more information there is, the less likely consumers are to take notice. This is particularly the case with complex ethical issues.

This complexity is increased by the amount of conflicting information produced by NGOs (non-governmental organisations): cotton is bad for the environment according to some scientific research bodies, good according to others; bamboo is ethical in some expert quarters, unethical in others. When the experts can't agree on the big issues for fashion, it's that much easier for the consumer to turn a blind eye and buy another new shirt made of unsustainable cotton. In fact, psychologists and behavioural scientists even go so far as to suggest that ethical fashion consumerism may not be an attainable goal.

An alternative, radical solution might be to recognise that throughout history, humans have used fashionable clothes to satisfy emotional, egoistical desires. So the challenge should be shifted from trying to control these behaviours to finding a way to accommodate them. Instead of trying to appeal to the consumer's supposed ethical streak, perhaps brands should aim instead to use new technology and business models to design products that can be recycled or re-engineered into new styles with minimal consumption of virgin materials, water, energy and chemicals.

In this model, the aim would not be to change thousands of years of evolution, but rather to use innovation and creativity to make industry bend to people's inherent needs. It is a major technical and commercial challenge, but shifting to such consumer-driven model may open up new opportunities for business, as well as increasing sustainability.

groups.title: Obstacles to ethical fashion consumerism
content: There are a number of reasons why the predicted growth of ethical consumerism has not materialised in mainstream fashion. Consumers may not know about the issues involved or are {{30}} to spend money on sustainable products. Moreover, questionnaires and surveys used to forecast consumer trends have proved to be {{31}} When giving responses about ethical behaviour, some participants may be dishonest, while others are {{32}} of the factors influencing their decisions. Another cause of the failure of ethical consumerism is that shoppers tend to make choices that are both {{33}} and selfish, often driven by urges to seek out enjoyment and enhanced status. Furthermore, when faced with environmental information about products that is inconsistent, consumers feel more able to ignore the ethical advice of experts. For all of these reasons, some academics believe ethical fashion consumerism to be an {{34}} aim.
